Each of these has its own mimic, vasculitis or catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome for autoimmunity, fungemia or viremia in HIV and transplant patients, antirejection or GVHD drugs, severe hypertension causing endothelial injury, preeclampsia and HELLP in pregnancy, and drug induced TMA or tumor embolism in malignancy. But notice that atypical HUS, AHUS, appears in almost every single row as a differential. That's the exam pearl, complement mediated TMA can be unmasked or triggered by any of these systemic stressors, so a normal ADAMTS13 level in a sick patient with MAHA and thrombocytopenia should prompt you to think about AHUS and these comorbid triggers, not just assume it's not TTP and stop there. Management often involves excluding infection, adjusting the offending drug, biopsy when needed, and empiric anti C5 therapy for suspected AHUS.

keypoints: AHUS is a recurring differential across nearly every comorbid TMA trigger
Autoimmune disease, HIV, HSCT, solid organ transplant, malignant HTN, pregnancy, malignancy all cause MAHA + thrombocytopenia independent of TTP
Exclude infection and offending drugs before empiric anti-C5 therapy
Normal ADAMTS13 does not rule out AHUS
segments.voiceover: When MAHA and thrombocytopenia occur with autoimmune disease, HIV, transplant, malignant hypertension, pregnancy, or cancer, don't stop at ruling out TTP, atypical HUS shows up as a differential in nearly every one of these settings. Work up infection, review culprit drugs, consider biopsy, and think about empiric anti-C5 therapy for suspected complement mediated TMA once other causes are excluded.

This table gives the actual prevalence data behind the classic TTP pentad, and these numbers are worth memorizing because boards love asking which feature is most common versus least common. Neurologic symptoms are very common overall, headache and confusion occur in about sixty percent of patients, and if you break neurologic findings down, mild deficits like headache or confusion occur in about twenty five percent while severe findings, coma, focal deficits, or seizures, occur in fully fifty percent, so when neurologic involvement happens in TTP it tends to be severe. Renal involvement is the opposite pattern, mild proteinuria or renal insufficiency is common at forty percent, but severe acute renal failure is uncommon, only about five percent, which is a key differentiator from HUS where renal failure dominates. Digestive symptoms, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, occur in about half of patients and can mimic other diagnoses early on. Bleeding symptoms like purpura or menorrhagia are seen in only twenty percent, since TTP is primarily a thrombotic, not a hemorrhagic, disorder despite the low platelet count. And the hematologic numbers are dramatic, platelet counts under twenty times ten to the ninth per liter in ninety five percent of patients, and hemoglobin under eight in eighty percent, reflecting severe consumptive thrombocytopenia and hemolysis.

keypoints: Headache/confusion ~60%; severe neuro findings (coma, seizures, focal deficits) ~50%
Severe renal failure only ~5% in TTP, unlike HUS
Platelet count <20 in 95%; hemoglobin <8 in 80%
Bleeding symptoms only ~20% -- TTP is thrombotic, not hemorrhagic
segments.voiceover: Lock in these TTP prevalence numbers for boards, headache or confusion in sixty percent, with severe neurologic findings like coma or seizures in fully half of patients. Renal failure is usually mild, severe renal failure occurs in only about five percent, which helps distinguish TTP from HUS. Platelets drop below twenty in ninety five percent of patients and hemoglobin falls below eight in eighty percent, while overt bleeding is uncommon at only twenty percent.

This smear is the single most important morphology image for TMA on the boards, and you need to be able to spot these findings instantly. The arrows point to schistocytes, fragmented red blood cells that form when RBCs are sheared apart passing through vessels partially occluded by platelet rich microthrombi, and helmet cells, a specific schistocyte shape with a crescent, helmet like outline. These fragments are the morphologic signature of mechanical intravascular hemolysis, and finding more than about one percent schistocytes on a smear in the right clinical context is essentially required to diagnose MAHA. You'll also see polychromasia, larger bluish gray red cells reflecting a robust reticulocyte response to the ongoing hemolysis, and occasional nucleated RBCs, which signal marrow stress from severe hemolysis pushing out immature erythroid precursors early. Finally notice the striking absence of platelets on this field, consistent with the severe consumptive thrombocytopenia of TTP or other TMAs, since platelets are being consumed to form the microvascular thrombi. On an exam, if you're shown a smear like this with fragments and no platelets, your differential should immediately jump to TMA, and specifically TTP if severe thrombocytopenia and neurologic findings are present without another clear cause.

keypoints: Schistocytes and helmet cells = mechanical hemolysis signature
Polychromasia = brisk reticulocyte response to hemolysis
Nucleated RBCs reflect marrow stress
Absent/scant platelets on smear = consumptive thrombocytopenia
segments.voiceover: On boards, recognize schistocytes and helmet cells instantly as the morphologic fingerprint of microangiopathic hemolysis, RBCs sheared apart by microvascular thrombi. Polychromasia shows the marrow is responding with reticulocytes, and nucleated red cells signal marrow stress. The scarcity of platelets on the field reflects consumptive thrombocytopenia, and together these findings should trigger a TMA workup.

This slide gets into the molecular mechanism that underlies TTP, and it's a favorite for board questions on ADAMTS13 biology. On the left, under flowing blood, VWF strings anchored to the vessel wall recruit platelets through the platelet receptor GPIb, and ADAMTS13, the metalloprotease, sits right at that site to regulate VWF length. On the right is the domain map of VWF, with the A1 domain binding GPIb and collagen, the A2 domain containing the actual ADAMTS13 cleavage site at tyrosine 1605 to methionine 1606, and the A3 domain also binding collagen. The critical concept is that ADAMTS13 can only access and cleave that Tyr1605-Met bond in the A2 domain when VWF is unfolded by shear force, shown here by the arrows labeled Force pulling the A2 domain open. Under high shear in the microcirculation, VWF stretches out, exposing the cleavage site, and ADAMTS13 trims the ultra large multimers down to a manageable size. If ADAMTS13 is deficient or inhibited, as in TTP, those ultra large VWF multimers stay uncleaved and hyperreactive, recruiting excessive platelets and driving microvascular thrombosis. Know that ADAMTS13 itself has a modular structure too, metalloprotease, disintegrin, thrombospondin repeats, cysteine rich and spacer domains, and CUB domains, which mediate substrate recognition.

keypoints: ADAMTS13 cleaves VWF at Tyr1605-Met1606 within the A2 domain
Cleavage site is exposed only when shear force unfolds A2
A1 domain binds GPIb/collagen; A3 binds collagen
ADAMTS13 deficiency = uncleaved ultra-large VWF multimers -> platelet hyperaggregation
segments.voiceover: For boards, know that ADAMTS13 cleaves VWF specifically at tyrosine 1605 to methionine within the A2 domain, and this site is only exposed when shear force unfolds VWF in flowing blood. The A1 domain mediates platelet GPIb and collagen binding, while A3 binds collagen. When ADAMTS13 is deficient, ultra large VWF multimers go uncleaved, staying hyperadhesive and driving excessive platelet recruitment, which is the molecular basis of TTP.

This figure ties together everything about ADAMTS13 into the actual pathogenesis of TTP, and it's essentially a must know diagram for boards. On the left, under normal flowing blood, VWF multimers are anchored to the vessel wall and platelets attach through GPIb, forming small platelet VWF aggregates. What happens next branches into two pathways depending on ADAMTS13. When ADAMTS13 is present and functional, it continuously cleaves the stretched VWF, limiting how large these platelet aggregates can grow, so platelets and VWF fragments are released back into circulation, this is normal hemostasis, a self limited, regulated process. But when ADAMTS13 is absent or severely deficient, whether from an inherited mutation as in congenital TTP or an autoantibody as in acquired immune TTP, there is nothing to cleave the VWF, so platelet VWF aggregation continues unchecked. The bottom right panel shows the result, massive, uncontrolled platelet rich thrombi building up on the vessel wall, which is exactly what causes the diffuse microvascular thrombosis of TTP, consuming platelets, causing mechanical hemolysis as red cells shear through the narrowed vessels, and producing ischemic organ injury in the brain, kidneys, heart, and elsewhere. This single figure explains why plasma exchange, which replaces functional ADAMTS13 and removes autoantibody, is the cornerstone emergency treatment for acquired TTP.

keypoints: ADAMTS13 present: cleaves stretched VWF, limits platelet aggregate size, normal hemostasis
ADAMTS13 absent (mutation or autoantibody): unchecked VWF-platelet aggregation
Result: diffuse microvascular platelet-VWF thrombi = TTP
Explains why plasma exchange (replace ADAMTS13, remove autoantibody) is first-line TTP therapy
segments.voiceover: This figure is the core pathogenesis diagram for TTP. With functional ADAMTS13, VWF gets cleaved as it stretches, capping platelet aggregate size, that's normal hemostasis. Without ADAMTS13, from either a genetic mutation or an autoantibody, VWF-platelet aggregation runs unchecked, building the diffuse microvascular thrombi that define TTP. This is exactly why plasma exchange, restoring ADAMTS13 and clearing the autoantibody, is emergency first-line therapy.

This table compares the two most commonly tested clinical prediction scores for identifying severe ADAMTS13 deficiency, meaning iTTP, in patients presenting with microangiopathic hemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia. The PLASMIC score has seven components, each worth one point: platelet count under thirty times ten to the ninth per liter, creatinine under two milligrams per deciliter, evidence of hemolysis defined as indirect bilirubin over two, reticulocytes over two point five percent, or undetectable haptoglobin, INR under one point five, MCV under ninety femtoliters, no active cancer, and no history of solid organ or stem cell transplant. A PLASMIC score of five or higher has a sensitivity of ninety-nine percent and specificity of fifty-seven percent for severe ADAMTS13 deficiency, making it the preferred bedside tool because it's highly sensitive and easy to calculate before ADAMTS13 results return. The modified French score uses just two variables, platelet count under thirty and creatinine under two point two six, and a score of one or higher has sensitivity of ninety-eight point eight percent but much lower specificity at forty-eight percent. For boards, know that PLASMIC is the more widely used and validated score, that both scores are meant to rapidly triage patients for empiric plasma exchange while awaiting ADAMTS13 activity, and that low specificity means these scores overcall TTP, so ADAMTS13 testing remains essential to confirm the diagnosis.

keypoints: PLASMIC: 7 factors, score ≥5 → 99% sens, 57% spec for severe ADAMTS13 deficiency
Components: plt <30, Cr <2, hemolysis, INR <1.5, MCV <90, no cancer, no transplant
French score: 2 factors (plt <30, Cr <2.26), score ≥1 → 98.8% sens, 48% spec
High sensitivity scores triage for empiric plasma exchange pending ADAMTS13
segments.voiceover: PLASMIC is the seven-factor score, and a score of five or higher gives ninety-nine percent sensitivity for severe ADAMTS13 deficiency, though specificity is only fifty-seven percent. Its components are low platelets, low creatinine, evidence of hemolysis, a near-normal INR, a normal MCV, and the absence of active cancer or transplant history. The modified French score is simpler, just platelets and creatinine, with similarly high sensitivity around ninety-nine percent but even lower specificity near forty-eight percent. Both are designed to be highly sensitive so you don't miss iTTP, which is why they drive the decision to start empiric plasma exchange while confirmatory ADAMTS13 activity testing is pending.

This algorithm walks through management of suspected immune TTP based on pretest probability and ADAMTS13 results. Patients with high probability of iTTP, meaning a high PLASMIC or French score, should start therapeutic plasma exchange, steroids, and caplacizumab immediately while sending ADAMTS13 activity, because delaying treatment for confirmatory testing risks mortality. Patients with low to intermediate probability start TPE and steroids alone, holding caplacizumab until the diagnosis is more certain, since caplacizumab carries bleeding risk and shouldn't be used empirically in low-probability patients. Once ADAMTS13 activity results return, they reclassify patients into three groups. A positive result, ADAMTS13 activity under ten percent, confirms iTTP, so you continue TPE, steroids, and caplacizumab, and add rituximab for durable B-cell depletion and remission. A borderline result, ten to twenty percent, requires clinical judgement and consideration of alternative diagnoses like DIC, malignant hypertension, or complement-mediated TMA. A negative result, greater than twenty percent, essentially rules out iTTP, so you stop TPE, steroids, rituximab, and caplacizumab, and pursue other diagnoses. For boards, the key numbers are ADAMTS13 activity under ten percent confirms severe deficiency, and most true initial iTTP episodes have activity under five percent or undetectable, while relapsing episodes can have somewhat higher activity.

keypoints: High probability → start TPE + steroids + caplacizumab immediately, don't wait for ADAMTS13
Low-intermediate probability → TPE + steroids only, hold caplacizumab
ADAMTS13 <10% (positive) → continue triple therapy + add rituximab
ADAMTS13 >20% (negative) → stop all iTTP-specific therapy, consider other diagnoses
Most initial iTTP episodes: ADAMTS13 <5% or undetectable
segments.voiceover: For high-probability iTTP, start plasma exchange, steroids, and caplacizumab right away without waiting for ADAMTS13 results, since treatment delay is dangerous. Lower-probability patients get plasma exchange and steroids only, holding caplacizumab given its bleeding risk. Once ADAMTS13 activity returns, a positive result under ten percent confirms the diagnosis, so you continue all three therapies and add rituximab. A negative result above twenty percent means you stop everything and look for another cause. Remember that most true initial iTTP cases have ADAMTS13 activity under five percent or completely undetectable.

This figure illustrates the mechanism of action of caplacizumab, and it's a classic boards diagram for understanding iTTP pathophysiology and targeted therapy. In panel A, showing the pathogenesis of acquired TTP, anti-ADAMTS13 autoantibodies inhibit the enzyme's normal proteolytic cleavage of ultra-large von Willebrand factor multimers. Without cleavage, these ultra-large vWF strands persist and their A1 domain becomes activated, allowing platelets to bind through the glycoprotein Ib-alpha receptor. This drives excessive platelet aggregation, causing microvascular thrombosis and ischemic organ damage, which is the direct mechanistic explanation for the anemia, thrombocytopenia, and end-organ injury seen in TTP. Panel B shows how caplacizumab intervenes. Caplacizumab is a bivalent nanobody that binds directly to the A1 domain of von Willebrand factor, blocking the interaction between vWF and the platelet glycoprotein Ib-alpha receptor. This doesn't fix the underlying ADAMTS13 deficiency or remove the autoantibody, but it rapidly stops new microthrombi from forming, which is why caplacizumab produces fast platelet count recovery and reduces the risk of refractory TTP and exacerbations, even though ADAMTS13 activity and the autoantibody take longer to normalize with steroids, rituximab, and plasma exchange.

keypoints: ADAMTS13 autoantibody → unable to cleave ultra-large vWF → platelet-vWF microthrombi
Platelets bind ultra-large vWF via GPIb-α on the activated A1 domain
Caplacizumab = anti-vWF nanobody, blocks A1 domain-GPIb-α interaction
Stops new microthrombi fast, but doesn't treat the ADAMTS13 antibody itself
Explains why caplacizumab speeds platelet recovery but rituximab treats the autoimmune driver
segments.voiceover: In iTTP, autoantibodies against ADAMTS13 prevent cleavage of ultra-large von Willebrand factor, so these giant multimers stay intact and their A1 domain becomes activated, recruiting platelets through glycoprotein Ib-alpha and forming microthrombi. Caplacizumab is a nanobody that binds the A1 domain of von Willebrand factor directly, physically blocking that platelet interaction. It rapidly halts new clot formation and speeds platelet recovery, but it doesn't touch the underlying autoantibody, which is why it's paired with steroids and rituximab to treat the actual autoimmune process.

This table lists the clinical conditions most frequently associated with disseminated intravascular coagulation, and it's high-yield because boards love asking you to match the trigger to the predominant clinical phenotype, bleeding versus thrombosis. Severe infection, whether gram-positive, gram-negative, malaria, or hemorrhagic fevers, is probably the most common DIC trigger overall, and here thrombosis often contributes to organ failure such as acute kidney injury. Malignancy is another major cause, with solid tumors like adenocarcinomas typically producing a chronic, thrombotic phenotype with venous thromboembolism, while acute promyelocytic leukemia is the classic exception, causing severe thrombocytopenia and factor deficiency that leads to catastrophic bleeding, so APL and DIC is a very testable pairing. Trauma, including multitrauma, brain injury, and burns, has a biphasic course, acute bleeding first followed later by thrombosis. Obstetric complications like abruptio placentae and amniotic fluid embolism produce profuse bleeding combined with thrombotic complications. Vascular malformations such as Kasabach-Merritt syndrome cause bleeding from severe thrombocytopenia and hypofibrinogenemia. Finally, heat stroke and post-cardiopulmonary resuscitation states are notable because thrombotic features predominate over bleeding, which is a useful discriminator on exams.

keypoints: Sepsis is the most common DIC trigger; often drives organ failure via thrombosis
APL (acute promyelocytic leukemia): classic cause of severe bleeding DIC
Solid tumors: chronic, thrombotic DIC phenotype (VTE)
Trauma: biphasic - acute bleeding then thrombosis
Kasabach-Merritt, heat stroke, post-CPR: distinct bleeding vs thrombotic patterns
segments.voiceover: Sepsis is the leading cause of DIC and tends to drive organ failure through thrombosis. Acute promyelocytic leukemia is the classic malignancy causing a severe bleeding-predominant DIC, in contrast to solid tumors, which usually produce a chronic thrombotic phenotype with venous thromboembolism. Trauma causes a biphasic pattern, bleeding acutely and thrombosis later, while obstetric catastrophes like abruptio placentae combine both. Remember heat stroke and post-cardiac arrest states as conditions where thrombosis, not bleeding, is the dominant feature of DIC.

This clinical image shows a patient with severe DIC-related coagulopathy manifesting as extensive purpura fulminans-like skin necrosis. You can see dusky, violaceous, and frankly necrotic discoloration involving the hand, forearm, and lower leg, with surgical marking outlining areas likely being assessed for debridement or amputation, along with a critically ill, intubated patient in the bottom right panel. This pattern reflects the microvascular thrombosis component of DIC, where widespread fibrin deposition in small dermal and subdermal vessels causes ischemic skin necrosis, classically seen in severe sepsis, meningococcemia, or other fulminant infections triggering consumptive coagulopathy. Simultaneously, consumption of platelets and clotting factors, along with fibrinolysis, produces the bleeding component, which is why DIC is fundamentally a disease of simultaneous clotting and bleeding rather than one or the other. For boards, recognize this presentation as symmetric peripheral gangrene or purpura fulminans, associate it with severe sepsis-induced DIC, and remember that these patients often require ICU-level support, source control, and may need surgical debridement or amputation of necrotic tissue despite treatment of the underlying coagulopathy.

keypoints: Purpura fulminans / symmetric peripheral gangrene = severe DIC manifestation
Caused by widespread microvascular fibrin thrombosis with ischemic skin necrosis
Classically triggered by severe sepsis or meningococcemia
DIC = simultaneous thrombosis AND consumptive bleeding, not just one
May require debridement or amputation despite treating underlying coagulopathy
segments.voiceover: This image shows purpura fulminans, or symmetric peripheral gangrene, a severe manifestation of DIC where widespread microvascular fibrin thrombosis causes ischemic skin necrosis, classically triggered by severe sepsis or meningococcemia. It's a vivid reminder that DIC is simultaneously a thrombotic and a bleeding disorder, driven by consumption of platelets and clotting factors alongside ongoing fibrin deposition. Despite treating the underlying trigger and coagulopathy, extensive tissue necrosis like this often requires surgical debridement or amputation.

This case shows a thirty-four year old woman with choriocarcinoma, multiple metastases, and DIC, illustrating acral ischemic necrosis of the fingers and toes, with dark purple-black discoloration of the distal digits and surrounding petechial hemorrhage on the dorsum of the hand and foot. Choriocarcinoma is a gestational trophoblastic malignancy that's highly vascular and prone to both hemorrhage and thromboembolic complications, and when it triggers DIC, patients develop this combination of digital ischemia from microvascular thrombosis alongside petechiae and ecchymoses from the consumptive bleeding diathesis. This case reinforces the malignancy-associated DIC category from the earlier table, and it's a good reminder that gestational trophoblastic disease, though rare, is a boards-favorite cause of DIC in a woman of reproductive age, especially when paired with an elevated beta-hCG and pulmonary or CNS metastases. The digital gangrene pattern here, distinct from the more confluent purpura fulminans on the prior slide, still reflects the same underlying pathophysiology of fibrin thrombus formation in the microvasculature superimposed on a bleeding tendency from factor and platelet consumption.

keypoints: 34F, choriocarcinoma with metastases, complicated by DIC
Digital ischemic necrosis (fingers/toes) + petechiae = combined thrombotic-bleeding DIC picture
Choriocarcinoma: highly vascular gestational trophoblastic tumor, prone to DIC
Consider GTD/choriocarcinoma as a DIC cause in reproductive-age women with high beta-hCG
segments.voiceover: This is a thirty-four year old woman with metastatic choriocarcinoma complicated by DIC, showing dark ischemic necrosis of the fingers and toes alongside petechial bleeding. Choriocarcinoma is a highly vascular gestational trophoblastic tumor that can trigger DIC through the same combined thrombotic and consumptive bleeding mechanism seen in other malignancies. Keep gestational trophoblastic disease on your differential for DIC in a reproductive-age woman, particularly with a markedly elevated beta-hCG.

This is the ISTH scoring algorithm for overt DIC, and you need to know it cold for boards. It's built on four simple labs. Platelet count gets zero points if over 100, one point if under 100, and two points if under 50. Fibrin-related markers like D-dimer score zero if not increased, two points if increased but less than five times upper limit of normal, and three points if strongly increased at five times or more. Prolonged PT scores zero if under three seconds prolongation, one point for three to under six seconds, and two points for six seconds or more. Fibrinogen scores one point only if it's low, at or below one gram per liter, otherwise zero. Add up the points. A total score of five or greater is compatible with overt DIC. If the score comes back under five but you still suspect DIC clinically, the key pearl is to repeat the panel in one to two days rather than dismissing the diagnosis. Remember this algorithm is only valid in a patient who already has an underlying condition known to cause DIC, such as sepsis, trauma, or malignancy, so it is not a screening test for the general population.

keypoints: ISTH DIC score: platelets, fibrin markers, PT, fibrinogen
Score ≥5 = compatible with overt DIC
Fibrinogen ≤1.0 g/L = 1 pt; score <5 → repeat in 1-2 days
Only valid with a known DIC-associated underlying disorder
segments.voiceover: Know the four components of the ISTH DIC score: platelet count, fibrin-related markers like D-dimer, prothrombin time, and fibrinogen. A total of five or more points is compatible with overt DIC. Platelets score zero above 100, one below 100, two below 50 times ten to the ninth per liter. Fibrinogen only adds a point when it's at or below one gram per liter. If the score is under five but suspicion remains high, repeat testing in one to two days. And remember, this tool only applies to patients with an underlying disorder already known to be associated with DIC.

This flowchart is the practical companion to the ISTH score and it's exactly how boards like to test DIC management. Start with clinical suspicion, meaning a known DIC-associated condition plus a low or falling platelet count and prolonged PT or aPTT. Apply the DIC scoring algorithm. If the score is under five, there's no DIC, but repeat testing in one to two days if suspicion persists. If the score is five or greater, that's compatible with DIC, and the single most important step is always to treat the underlying condition, whether that's sepsis, obstetric catastrophe, or malignancy. Beyond that, management branches into three clinical scenarios. If the patient has active bleeding or needs an invasive procedure, give platelets to keep the count above 30 to 50, plasma or factor concentrates to keep the PT under three seconds and fibrinogen above 1.5, vitamin K if deficiency is suspected, and antifibrinolytics only if there's excessive hyperfibrinolysis. If there's no major bleeding or thrombosis, just give prophylactic low molecular weight heparin. And if the picture is overt thrombosis or organ failure from clot formation, like purpura fulminans, that calls for therapeutic anticoagulation, typically intravenous unfractionated heparin. The high-yield concept here is that DIC treatment is tailored to the dominant phenotype, bleeding versus clotting, not a one-size-fits-all protocol.

keypoints: Treat the underlying condition first, always
Bleeding/procedure: platelets, plasma/factor concentrate, ± vitamin K, antifibrinolytics only if hyperfibrinolysis
No bleeding/thrombosis: prophylactic LMW heparin
Thrombosis/organ failure (e.g. purpura fulminans): therapeutic heparin
Score <5: repeat DIC panel in 1-2 days

Active bleeding or a planned invasive procedure calls for platelet transfusion above 30 to 50, plasma or factor concentrate to correct PT and fibrinogen, vitamin K if indicated, and antifibrinolytics reserved for excessive hyperfibrinolysis. No major bleeding or clotting simply gets prophylactic low molecular weight heparin. Overt thrombosis or organ failure, like purpura fulminans, needs therapeutic anticoagulation. And if the initial score is under five, repeat it in one to two days rather than ruling out DIC outright.

This slide shows the classic clinical spectrum of hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, also called Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome, an autosomal dominant vascular disorder. Panels A and B show mucocutaneous telangiectasias, small blanching red spots on the lip, tongue, and fingertips, which are the most visible and earliest clue on exam. But the boards-relevant danger is visceral involvement, shown in panels C and D. Panel C is a chest x-ray and panel D is a pulmonary angiogram demonstrating a pulmonary arteriovenous malformation, a direct right-to-left shunt between a pulmonary artery and vein that bypasses the capillary bed. These pulmonary AVMs matter enormously because they create a paradoxical embolism risk, meaning clots or even bacteria can cross straight to the systemic circulation and cause stroke or brain abscess without ever passing through the lung filter. HHT patients also commonly have GI telangiectasias causing occult bleeding and iron deficiency anemia, plus hepatic AVMs. So the pattern to remember is mucocutaneous telangiectasias plus recurrent epistaxis plus visceral AVMs, especially pulmonary, hepatic, and cerebral.

Mucocutaneous telangiectasias: lips, tongue, fingertips (A, B)
Pulmonary AVM (C, D): right-to-left shunt
Pulmonary AVM → paradoxical embolism → stroke, brain abscess
Also screen for hepatic and GI AVMs/telangiectasias
